CDF Munir, Singapore's FM discuss regional security and bilateral cooperation
items.description: Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir met with Singapore’s Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan on Friday, where the two discussed regional security and avenues for bilateral cooperation, according to the military’s media wing. In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the foreign minister, who is currently in the country on an official visit, called on CDF Munir at the General Headquarters (GHQ) in Rawalpindi. The two leaders discussed matters of mutual interest, evolving regional and global security dynamics and avenues for bilateral cooperation, it said. “Both sides exchanged views on regional peace and stability and underscored the importance of sustained engagement and cooperation in areas of shared interest,” the statement read. During the meeting, CDF Munir reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to strengthening bilateral relations with Singapore, including enhancing “institutional linkages and constructive engagement for promoting regional peace, stability and security”. The Singaporean diplomat reciprocated the commitment and lauded the professionalism of Pakistan’s armed forces. He acknowledged Pakistan’s role in regional peace and stability, ISPR added. PM admires Singapore’s ‘remarkable economic transformation’ Earlier, the foreign minister met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, during which the premier expressed admiration for Singapore’s “remarkable economic transformation” and achievements in innovation and development. According to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), the premier reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening its longstanding and friendly relations with Singapore, particularly as the two countries are commemorating the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations this year. “The prime minister expressed admiration for Singapore’s remarkable economic transformation and achievements in innovation and development. He underscored the importance Pakistan attaches to its partnership with Singapore, both bilaterally and multilaterally including within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean),” it said. The statement said that the two sides discussed ways to enhance bilateral trade and investment and expand cooperation in priority areas, including the digital economy, fintech, infrastructure development, logistics, small and medium enterprises and the services sector. They also discussed exploring new avenues for mutually beneficial economic cooperation and enhancing people-to-people contacts. “The two sides also exchanged views on regional and international developments and reaffirmed their commitment to continued engagement and cooperation at bilateral and multilateral fora,” it said. Possible resumption of direct flights discussed The meetings came shortly after Dar discussed with the visiting diplomat the possible resumption of direct flights between Pakistan and Singapore “to facilitate business travel and close contact between our peoples”. Dar shared this while addressing a press conference alongside Balakrishnan. He began by saying that Pakistan and Singapore enjoyed longstanding and friendly ties focused on mutual respect and goodwill, and Pakistan was one of the first countries to recognise Singapore following its independence in 1965. He noted that Balakrishnan’s visit to Pakistan was the first one by a Singaporean foreign minister in over two decades. “I am grateful that he was kind to accept my invitation,” he said, adding that the trip was particularly significant as the two countries were commemorating 60 years of diplomatic relations this year. “The visit reflects our shared commitment to strengthen this friendship and broaden our cooperation.” Dar said that delegation-level talks and a restricted meeting between the two sides earlier in the day focused on strengthening political and economic ties, expanding cooperation in technology and education and promoting culture and people-to-people contact. “We also exchanged views on key regional and international developments,” he added. He further stated that the two sides had recognised “the considerable untapped potential in our relationship” and stressed the importance of sustained engagement. “We agreed to hold regular bilateral political consultation and promote high-level exchanges to strengthen cooperation between our governments and institutions,” he said, adding that economic cooperation was central to the discussions. He said “we welcomed the significant growth” in bilateral trade between the two countries and discussed ways to build on this progress further. “We agreed to encourage closer engagement between our business communities through the exchange of business delegations and stronger links between our chambers of commerce,” he elaborated. Moreover, Dar continued, the reopening of the Trade and Investment Office at Pakistan’s High Commission in Singapore had also been discussed. “The reopening of the Pakistan Trade and Investment Office is a testament to Pakistan’s resolve to promote stronger B2B ties with our friendly country Singapore.” Beyond trade and investment, he said: “We discussed the scope for closer cooperation in education, research and innovation, including digital technologies and artificial intelligence. We also considered ways to strengthen links between our universities and research institutions. We also agreed to deepen cooperation in human resource development, agriculture and climate domains.” Dar noted that Pakistani professionals in Singapore contributed to its economy and society and served as a “valuable bridge between our two nations”. He said, “We agreed to encourage greater cultural, academic, youth and people-to-people exchanges.” Moreover, he said, “We also discussed the possible resumption of direct flights to facilitate business travel and close contact between our peoples.” Pakistan’s engagement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) as the country’s “oldest sectoral dialogue partner” also came under discussion, Dar said. “Pakistan attaches great importance to practical cooperation with the organisation and its member states. I convey Pakistan’s best wishes to Singapore as it prepares to assume the Asean chairmanship in 2027. “We look forward to working closely with Singapore in support of its priorities as the chair and to further strengthening the Pakistan-Asean cooperation.” Dar said the meetings in Islamabad also presented the opportunity to share perspectives on regional and international peace and the security landscape. “We discussed the impact of regional tensions on maritime trade,” he said, adding that secure sea routes and uninterrupted supply chains were essential to trade and economic stability. He said the two sides had reaffirmed the central role of dialogue and diplomacy, respect for international law and adherence to the principles of the UN Charter in addressing regional and global challenges. The DPM said he had conveyed to the visiting dignitary that Pakistan remained engaged with key regional and international partners to encourage continued dialogue and diplomacy as it was the “only viable means to resolve outstanding challenges”. On Palestine, he said, “I expressed concern over the continued expansion of illegal settlements and efforts to alter the status of the West Bank and Al-Quds Al-Sharif. I stressed the urgent need for unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance to the people of Gaza. I reiterated firm support for an independent, sovereign, viable, and contiguous state of Palestine based on pre-June 1967 borders with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital, which is the stated policy of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan”. In the context of South Asia, Dar said he briefed the visiting dignitary on the importance of a “just, durable and peaceful settlement of the longstanding Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with the relevant UN Security Council resolutions”. He concluded his speech by saying: “We look forward to working very closely with Singapore to carry forward the understanding reached today. Pakistan and Singapore’s friendship remains strong and forward-looking as we mark 60 years of diplomatic relations. “We have committed to deepening this partnership and building a more prosperous future for our people.” Speaking after him, Balakrishnan began by saying: “This is a significant year for Singapore and Pakistan. We have never forgotten that Pakistan was one of the earliest countries to recognise Singapore’s independence. And that’s why we are commemorating the 60th anniversary of diplomatic ties.” Over the years, he said, there had been high-level exchanges between the two countries. He added that “we’ve had opportunities for a substantive and productive exchange of views”. “We’re in constant communication, far more than people realise — that we have a very effective partnership.” Balakrishnan continued that Pakistan and Singapore had “excellent ties” at the diplomatic level. “In fact, they are so good that it makes it even more obvious that actual trade relations — and looking at the numbers and the data — ought to be much higher. And that, I would say, is the first order of business. “We need to facilitate greater trade and investment flows. We need to strengthen the links, especially between SMEs, between businessmen, and they need to meet, they need to know each other, they need to understand the business opportunities and the risks on both sides in Southeast Asia as well as South Asia,” he added. Balakrishnan said governments of the two countries needed to facilitate these interactions and identify new opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation. “In an increasingly uncertain global environment, including on the business side of it, I think it is all the more important for our two countries to remain open, connected and constructively engaged with each other,” he said. The two sides, he said, also discussed carbon markets, which “we think is another fertile opportunity for Singapore and Pakistan to work together”. “It will be another promising avenue to attract investments into projects in Pakistan that reduce emissions while supporting sustainable development, and our officials are exploring opportunities in this area.” Speaking about the exchange of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on disaster management between Singapore and Pakistan, he said it reflected “our shared commitment to strengthen disaster preparedness and response”. Disasters, he said, were not something one wished for. “But it is something which we have to prepare for and to be acutely aware that at the rate things are going, and with the progression of climate change, this is a current and clear threat. And the more we can work together and prepare together, the more resilient we will be”. Unfortunately, Pakistan had extensive experience in responding to large-scale natural disasters, Balakrishnan said, adding that Singapore could learn from Pakistan in how to cope with disasters and be more resilient for the future. “Through this MoU, we hope to explore cooperation in areas including early warning systems, the sharing of best practices, strengthening search and rescue capabilities, as well as hopefully conducting joint training and exercises. “It’s again worth remembering that disasters do not respect boundaries, do not have passports, and again, the more we can work together, the better,” he added. Moreover, the Singaporean foreign minister said “we welcome the opportunities to deepen cooperation between our institutes of higher learning, which includes the Nanyang Technological University and the National University of Singapore with Pakistan’s National University of Sciences and Technology”. “I want to emphasise that this is just the beginning. We hope to expand that list in due time.” On regional and international developments, he congratulated Dar for the “incredibly valuable role that Pakistan is playing”. “For instance, we know there is crisis in the Gulf, and in fact, most of the energy that comes through the Gulf is actually headed to the east — South Asia, Southeast Asia, and to Northeast Asia. “And the unique, but very constructive and valuable role that Pakistan plays is the one which we commend you for, and we wish you every success because if you succeed, it’s good for all of us.” He emphasised that international law was critical for both Pakistan and Singapore. And in the case of Singapore, he said, “because we are an island city state and our trade volume is three times our GDP, the maritime arena is essential. And therefore, the United Nations Convention of the Law of the Sea 1982, which sets out the freedom of navigation and overflight, especially in straits used for international navigation as a right not by the grace of littoral powers — This is of acute importance to us, and we are very, very heartened that Pakistan stands in exactly the same position this issue with us”. He noted that Singapore would take the chairmanship of Asean next year while Pakistan was already the chair of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. This, he said, would present another set of opportunities for these two regional blocs, “two dynamic, diverse regional blocs, to look for opportunities to do together”. He then moved on to education, saying that opportunities in this area were also discussed. “We are living in an age of a new industrial revolution, AI and digital technologies, and it is essential to ensure that our young people have the relevant skills not for yesterday’s jobs, but for tomorrow’s jobs. “And so, this emphasis on skills and relevant qualifications and capability and human talent development is another very important area for cooperation between Pakistan and Singapore,” he added. Talks on enhancing trade, investment cooperation Earlier, Dar and Balakrishnan held talks and discussed ways to enhance cooperation in trade and investment, the Foreign Office (FO) said. Balakrishnan arrived in Islamabad earlier in the day. He called on DPM Dar at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The FO said in a statement that the two leaders reviewed the “longstanding and friendly relations” between Pakistan and Singapore as the two countries marked 60 years of diplomatic relations. They underscored the importance of sustained high-level exchanges and discussed ways to further enhance cooperation in trade, investment, connectivity and skills development, while promoting business-to-business exchanges and people-to-people contacts, the statement added. Dar and Balakrishnan also discussed cooperation at multilateral fora and Pakistan’s enhanced engagement with Asean, particularly in the context of Singapore’s forthcoming chairmanship of the body in 2027. Moreover, exchanging views on regional and global developments, Dar emphasised the importance of dialogue and diplomacy in resolving disputes and advancing lasting peace and stability, the statement said. Delegation-level talks Later, their opening remarks from delegation-level talks between the two sides were televised, with Dar saying that the depth of diplomatic relations between Pakistan and Singapore was not reflected in economic ties. He said his focus had been on “economic diplomacy” after joining the Foreign Office, adding: “If we work together, […] I am sure we can reach a new level of economic relations.” The DPM further suggested the Board of Investment in Pakistan could work with its counterpart in Singapore. He said the two countries had “great cooperation” on multilateral issues and Singapore’s interest in regional issues was “greatly appreciated”. “You remain in touch, and we keep sharing developments with you.” He added that the two had also discussed Palestine and Kashmir issues, among other matters, in a restricted meeting. “So I think this friendship and great cooperation will continue from our side, and I am sure you will always reciprocate, rather go a mile ahead of us,” the DPM said. For his part, the Singaporean foreign minister recalled that Pakistan was one of the “early countries to recognise Singapore post independence”. He pointed out that Singapore was 61 years old and was commemorating the 60th anniversary of diplomatic ties with Pakistan. According to the FO, the delegation-level talks focused on expanding trade and investment, strengthening cooperation in agriculture and food security and enhancing connectivity to promote tourism and business exchanges. “The two sides also explored collaboration in education, vocational training, disaster management and information technology. The Singaporean foreign minister highlighted the potential of carbon markets to attract green investment to Pakistan. Dar emphasised the importance of stronger institutional mechanisms and regular follow-up to advance mutually beneficial cooperation,” it said. “The Ministers also exchanged views on regional and global developments. Singapore’s foreign minister commended Pakistan’s sustained efforts to promote dialogue and diplomacy in the region and its important contributions to regional peace and stability,” it added. “Both sides agreed to build on the positive momentum generated by the visit, ensure timely follow-up on the understandings reached, and sustain engagement to further strengthen Pakistan-Singapore relations across all areas of mutual interest,” it said. After the meeting, Dar and Balakrishnan also exchanged an MoU on cooperation in disaster management between Pakistan’s National Disaster Management Authority and the Singapore Civil Defence Force in Islamabad. “The MoU reflects the shared commitment of Pakistan and Singapore to strengthening cooperation in disaster preparedness and response and building resilience against natural disasters,” the FO statement on the document’s exchange said.

items.title: NDC defends Obi’s single-term pledge, dismisses Okorocha’s ‘gambling’ claim
items.description: By Henry Umoru The National Leadership of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC has thrown its weight behind the single-term presidential pledge by its Presidential candidate ahead of January 16 2027. Peter Obi. The NDC described describing it as a constitutional commitment to performance, national stability and leadership accountability rather than a political gamble, adding that Obi had voluntarily offered to serve only one term, subjecting his leadership to public assessment based on results rather than political calculations. The party noted that Nigeria’s experience with an eight-year presidential administration between 2015 and 2023 demonstrated that longevity in office did not automatically translate into improved governance or national development, adding that the period was characterised by rising inflation, naira depreciation, increasing public debt, widespread poverty and insecurity In a statement signed on Friday by NDC Director-General of the National Presidential Campaign Council, NPCC, Mallam Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim, the party disagreed with Okorocha’s characterisation of the pledge as “a four-year gambling”, insisting that the proposal was constitutionally permissible and represented a deliberate commitment to deliver measurable results within four years. According to him, Section 135(2) of the 1999 Constitution provides for a four-year presidential tenure with the possibility of seeking another term, arguing that the provision does not make a second term compulsory. The leadership of the NDC was reacting to comments by former Imo State Governor, Senator Rochas Okorocha, during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today, where he described Obi as “a fantastic gentleman; clear in his head” but questioned the viability of his proposed single-term presidency. The party maintained that Obi’s single-term proposal was designed to shift the focus of presidential leadership from the duration of stay in office to measurable achievements and effective delivery of campaign promises. Describing the pledge as a performance commitment, He said, “Section 135(2) of the 1999 Constitution provides that a President shall leave office after four years and may seek a further four years. In law, ‘may’ is permissive, not mandatory. A single term is therefore constitutional. It is not a gamble. “Nigeria already tested an eight-year tenure between 2015 and 2023. The result was rising inflation, a weakened naira, soaring public debt, widespread poverty, and insecurity across the country. That is the real balance sheet of prolonged tenure without performance. “Peter Obi’s offer is a performance bond, not a gamble. He has pledged to serve one term, to be judged strictly by results, and to hand over power in 2031 in recognition that it is the turn of the North. This is sacrifice for national stability.” The Director-General noted that Nigeria’s governance challenges were not necessarily the result of insufficient time in office, but the failure of successive administrations to utilise available opportunities to deliver meaningful development. “Leadership is measured by impact, not duration. Nigeria’s problem has never been insufficient time. It has been the repeated failure to use time well. Mr. Obi proposes to reverse that culture: one term dedicated entirely to delivery,” Abdulkarim challenged Nigerians to assess the proposal from the perspective of accountability, insisting that a leader willing to limit his tenure despite being constitutionally eligible for another term was making a significant commitment to national service. “When a man entitled to eight years voluntarily chooses four and invites the nation to judge him by results, he is not gambling. He is sacrificing,” the statement said. The NDC said that Obi’s proposed single-term presidency should be understood as a time-bound commitment to national recovery and responsible leadership, adding, “This is not a gamble. It is a rescue mission with a deadline.” Vanguard News The post NDC defends Obi’s single-term pledge, dismisses Okorocha’s ‘gambling’ claim appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Redistricting Isn’t Going as Republicans Planned
items.description: D on Davis was born in Snow Hill, a small town on the coastal plains of North Carolina. Growing up, he spent Sundays worshipping at the local Presbyterian church and summers working in the surrounding tobacco fields. At 29, he was elected Snow Hill’s youngest-ever mayor. He went on to represent the town of about 1,500 in the state legislature and then in Congress. The Democrat is now running for a third term, but in a very different district: If he wins, his constituents will no longer include his wife, his kids, or anyone else in Snow Hill. Davis is used to having to figure out exactly who can vote for him. The first time he was elected to Congress, in 2022, he triumphed in a district that slightly favored Democrats. The North Carolina legislature redrew it to favor Republicans, and Davis won reelection in 2024 by less than two percentage points. Then, in the summer of 2025, President Trump called for the GOP to gerrymander as many seats as it could to protect the party’s House majority, even though redistricting is typically done only once a decade, after a census. Democrats in some states retaliated with their own gerrymanders. North Carolina was one of seven states, both red and blue, to hastily redraw its maps after Trump’s demand; four more redistricted after the Supreme Court’s April Louisiana v. Callais decision gutted the Voting Rights Act. Many of the incumbents being targeted for defeat by Republicans are Black Democrats. Davis, who had his home and base of support in surrounding Greene County cut out of his district, is one of them. But the gambit may not succeed as planned. Republicans are forecast to gain fewer than half of the seats they expected when they redrew the maps, in large part because voters are mad—over inflation, over corruption, over the Iran war . Here in North Carolina’s First Congressional District, many have an additional cause for anger: their gerrymandered map. The state, which is among the most politically divided in America, already has district lines that give Republicans a significant edge. The congressional delegation includes just four Democrats out of 14 representatives. The GOP-dominated legislature wants to cut that to three, and has drawn lines tailored to end Davis’s congressional career. If the new boundaries of his district had existed in 2024, Trump would have won the area by almost 12 points. (He carried the old district by just three.) The new map removed four counties with large Black populations and added six Republican-leaning ones near the state’s coast. Under the new map, the proportion of Black voters in the First District dropped from about 40 percent to about 32 percent. After the redistricting, the Cook Political Report labeled Davis “the most vulnerable House Democrat in the country.” He seemed like a goner. But recent polls show a close race, with both parties spending eye-popping amounts of money—more than $52.9 million in total, making it the most expensive House general election on record, according to the data-tracking firm AdImpact . Democrats have represented North Carolina’s First District since 1899, but Davis has been touting his centrist voting record in Congress. He often reminds voters that he has spent nearly all of his life in eastern North Carolina. “These are tobacco-cropping hands,” he told me, holding up his palms. (Federal law requires congressional candidates to live in the state, not the district, in which they are seeking office.) Davis is running against Republican Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel whom he narrowly beat in 2024. Buckhout is now trying to capitalize on the more deeply red composition of the district. “We are Republican-majority districts,” she told a crowd at a rally with President Trump and a Republican candidate in a nearby district last week. “That’s simple math. There are more of us. All you got to do is get out the vote.” After she left the stage, Trump turned to her: “You’re running against Don Davis? I hear he’s a total disaster.” It’s unclear if Trump’s support will help her. His popularity has cratered in the state; a recent poll from Elon University shows that only 34 percent of North Carolinians approve of the job he’s doing, despite the fact that he won 51 percent of the vote in 2024. Ben Lindemann was among the North Carolinians who voted for him. But the 49-year-old told me he will likely vote for Davis this year, in part because of the way Trump has governed. “I just don’t like the way he’s ruining our country,” Lindemann said. [ Read: The Republicans are bolting from Trump ] I n the past, Davis could count on votes from Greene County, where he ministers at the church he grew up attending. Now he needs to win over unaffiliated voters who may have never voted for a Democrat before in areas where he is less well-known. Billboards with his face line the highway: Don Davis supports lowering costs. Thank you Representative Davis, for supporting our veterans. There’s no mention of the Democratic Party; Davis, an Air Force veteran, is running as a brand unto himself. He often cites the times he’s crossed the aisle to vote with Republicans, including to end last year’s government shutdown, to fund ICE, and to condemn “socialism in all its forms.” In 2024, the website GovTrack, which assesses politicians’ voting records, ranked Davis the most conservative Democrat in the House. The district is among the most rural and agricultural in the state; seemingly endless fields of sweet potatoes and cotton line the sides of country roads. Davis was one of only 14 Democrats who voted in favor of this year’s Republican-sponsored Farm Bill, arguing that it would provide necessary support for the district’s economy. Farmers—particularly those who cultivate row crops such as tobacco and cotton—have been squeezed by tariffs and soaring operating costs. Thomas Joyner, a sweet-potato farmer, told me Davis is the only Democrat he’s ever voted for, because he “genuinely wants to help agriculture.” Richard Anderson, a 63-year-old who grows tobacco, told me Trump’s trade war with China destroyed the crop’s profitability by leaving a glut of product. He said he’ll be voting for Davis, even though he voted for Trump in 2024 and identifies as an independent. “I think that his district is proof that people will cross the aisle,” Anderson said. The gerrymander has given voters another reason to back Davis. People are angry about the redrawn lines, especially Black voters who feel the redistricting targeted them. Early votes cast by Black voters in North Carolina as of Wednesday were up 57 percent compared with the same date in 2022, according to the Election Lab at the University of Florida. Voting-rights advocates have said that a backlash against redistricting is driving a surge of African American turnout across the South. At the “Unapologetically Blue” banquet thrown by the Nash County Democratic Party earlier this month, more than 400 people showed up—the most in the event’s history, according to organizers. As I wandered among the crowd, attendees kept bringing up the unfairness of redistricting. “We fought hard for our rights. All of us did,” said 69-year-old Ernestine H. Stephenson, who is Black. Cynthia Pitchford told me that she grew up in the 1970s cropping tobacco; there were, she said, few other job options available for Black people in eastern North Carolina. Decades later, when Pitchford heard Davis was running for Congress, one of the first things she liked was their shared country background. This year, she decided to volunteer for him because she was so upset about the GOP’s gerrymandering. “I knew it was a ploy to try to pull votes away from him,” she said. [ Read: The arc of the Voting Rights Act ] I heard the same at the homecoming game of Elizabeth City State University, a historically Black university, where Davis walked the stands of the school’s football stadium in a driving rain, shaking hands with fans. He told me that people bring up redistricting all the time. “I believe the general feeling is that no one’s really asked for this,” Davis said. “I mean, people feel that they’re left out.” B uckhout lost to Davis in 2024 by only about 6,000 votes, and has since worked in a senior cyber-policy role in the Pentagon. She did not respond to my request for an interview, but when I talked with her supporters around the district, many said they believed she would fight socialism, which they said represents an existential threat to the country. Others applauded her military background and sense of patriotism. Buckhout spent decades in the Army and commanded an 800-person battalion in Iraq. “She’s strong and truthful,” said Rhonda Flood, a 61-year-old who has been volunteering for Buckhout’s campaign. Flood said the people she’s met while canvassing “know she’ll fight for the country, because she has.” Buckhout faces the same problem as many other Republicans this cycle—if your message is that the country is on the right track, how do you motivate voters who are unhappy with the state of the nation to show up? Early-voting numbers indicate that, so far, Republican turnout in North Carolina is lagging. Buckhout’s answer has been to campaign hard on fears about socialism and transgender issues. At the rally with Trump, she referenced ongoing unrest in France, warning that similar chaos could come to America if voters stop choosing Republicans. “I have fought against those people, and this is no joke,” she said to cheers. (When I asked the Buckhout campaign whom she meant by “those people,” the answer was “violent extremists.”) Buckhout has reminded voters that Davis in 2023 sponsored the Equality Act, which, if it had passed, would have banned discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity. She also criticizes him for being the only member of the House to vote “present,” rather than yea or nay, on a 2025 bill that would have effectively banned trans student athletes from playing in federally funded girls’ school sports. (Davis said the issue should be left up to states, not the federal government.) Several Republicans I spoke with said they are voting for Buckhout because of her opposition to transgender athletes. (Davis has said he supports North Carolina’s ban on transgender athletes.) In 2025, Davis was one of only three Democrats who supported former Republican Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene’s bill criminalizing gender-affirming care for minors. When I asked Davis if he still supported the Equality Act, he said his support had “evolved.” Davis opposed last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act—which Buckhout has touted on the campaign trail for its tax cuts and other help for working families. But as I traveled North Carolina, voters told me that the cost of living is surging at a relentless pace, and they were seeing little relief. [ Read: Going hungry in Trump’s economy ] The district once seemed an easy flip for Republicans. But in a year when the price of gas has spiked, tariffs are squeezing businesses, and some undecided voters are still trying to get to know the candidates, a redistricting plan that appeared to be a sure thing could backfire. If it does, Davis said he will leave Snow Hill and find a house within the district’s new lines.

items.title: 18e édition du salon international de l’artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO) : Le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ appelle à une révolution créative de l’artisanat
items.description: Le Chef de l’État a salué le talent et la créativité des artisans qui sont venus des quatre coins du continent africain Le Président du Faso, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, a présidé dans la matinée de ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou, la cérémonie d’ouverture de la 18e édition du Salon international de l’Artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO), qui se tient jusqu’au 8 novembre 2026, sous le thème : « Artisanat africain et industrialisation : quelle synergie pour une meilleure organisation et valorisation des produits locaux comme patrimoine culturel ? ». Après la coupure officielle du ruban de ce grand rendez-vous continental, le Président du Faso a réaffirmé son engagement à propulser l’artisanat africain au-delà du cadre traditionnel en l'orientant résolument vers la modernisation et l’industrialisation. « La vision, c'est de faire en sorte que notre artisanat progresse petit à petit vers une industrialisation. On ne peut pas avoir de métallurgie, de sidérurgie qui permettent de faire tout ce que vous faites, sans maîtriser la matière, sans avoir de l'art », a indiqué le Chef de l’État. « Nous ne voulons pas seulement que le monde admire ce que nos mains produisent ; nous voulons que nos peuples puissent vivre dignement de ce que leurs mains créent », a soutenu le Ministre de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat, le camarade Serge Gnaniodem PODA « Le Président Mahama, votre frère, m’a chargée de vous transmettre ses chaleureuses salutations et de vous faire part de l’importance capitale que le Ghana accorde à cette invitation ainsi qu’aux liens qui unissent nos deux nations », a indiqué la Ministre du Commerce, de l'Agroalimentaire et de l'Industrie du Ghana, pays invité d’honneur, Mme Elizabeth OFOSU-ADJARE au Chef de l’État Le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ a invité les artisans africains à être plus créatifs, à se perfectionner et « ne jamais baisser les bras, ne jamais penser que ce que les autres font est au-delà de ce qu'ils font ». Prononçant le discours d’ouverture du Président du Faso, le Ministre de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat, Serge Gnaniodem PODA, a souligné que la vision de la Révolution Progressiste Populaire est de faire de l’artisanat un outil de souveraineté et surtout d’épanouissement des acteurs du secteur. « La véritable indépendance se construit aussi dans nos ateliers, dans nos champs, dans nos usines et dans le choix quotidien de nos consommateurs », a précisé le Ministre PODA. La Ministre du Commerce, de l'Agroalimentaire et de l'Industrie du Ghana, pays invité d’honneur, Mme Elizabeth OFOSU-ADJARE, a apprécié l’honneur fait à son pays en l’associant à cette 18e édition du SIAO. items.title: L’après-Joj, c’est maintenant (Le billet de Omar DIOUF)
items.description: Dakar se fait belle ces dernières semaines. Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse 2026 oblige. Pour accueillir ses hôtes de marque, la capitale sénégalaise a commencé depuis des jours à déployer l’alchimie de la Téranga du pays. On balaie les rues, taille les arbres ; on remplace les pavés cassés, remblaie les nids de poule, et la circulation sera bientôt plus fluide, la sécurité est déjà en alerte. En voyant les lampadaires et de nouvelles décorations allumés, et le branle-bas d’efforts déployés ces derniers jours pour accueillir les jeunes athlètes et touristes du monde, un internaute s’est alors demandé, pourquoi les villes sénégalaises ne devraient pas être ainsi embellies quotidiennement ? À juste titre. Sans attendre l’organisation d’un événement international, nous nous devons de rendre nos cités avenantes, les transformer en endroits où il fait bon vivre. Et pourquoi pas commencer dès maintenant ce défi avec la généralisation des écoquartiers ? omar.diouf@lesoleil.sn

items.title: New US Sanctions Target Rwanda’s Abusive Role in Eastern Congo
items.description: Click to expand Image A member of the M23 looks on during an enrollment of civilians, police officers, and former members of the Congolese armed forces who have been recruited in Goma on February 23, 2025. © 2025 Michel Lunanga/AFP via Getty Images The United States Treasury announced new sanctions this week against Rwanda's Ministry of Defense and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution that the US Treasury found facilitated payments for the Rwandan army and the abusive M23 armed group. The sanctions freeze all named parties’ assets and interests in the US and effectively bar their use of the US dollar in international transactions. Thousands of Rwandan soldiers have fought alongside the M23 in eastern Congo since the group’s resurgence in late 2021. The Rwandan army has also provided the M23 with significant logistical and material support. In announcing the new sanctions, the US Treasury noted the M23 has perpetrated serious human rights abuses. The armed group has carried out unlawful killings, sexual violence, forced recruitment and forced labor, unlawful detentions, forced population transfers, and torture or other physical abuses in areas under its control. The treasury also stated that a Zigama branch enabled the transportation of gold sourced from rebel-controlled territory in eastern Congo to the Rwandan capital Kigali and facilitated financial transactions for the M23 worth tens of millions of dollars. While prior US sanctions issued in March targeted the Rwanda Defence Force and individual senior commanders, sanctioning the ministry targets the institution overseeing all military operations in support of M23. The sanctions come weeks after former Congolese president Joseph Kabila announced the creation of a political-military coalition that includes the M23, called the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (Front pour la Refondation de la Nation, FRN). Washington already sanctioned Kabila in April for his alleged support to armed groups. Sanctions alone, however will not protect civilians and should be accompanied by concrete measures to secure an end to abuses. The United Nations identified the M23 as the leading perpetrator of documented human rights violations in 2025, with the Congolese army second. The US and other governments should also press Congo to investigate and prosecute its own forces responsible for abuse, ensure they respect humanitarian law, and to end support for abusive groups. Above all, greater pressure is needed to ensure that protection of civilians and accountability are central to peace efforts.

items.title: Bill proposing quarterly gas pricing lands in Senate
items.description: ISLAMABAD: In what is set to stir a new controversy, a bill proposing quarterly determination of natural gas prices landed in the upper House of Parliament on Friday. The Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) (Amendment) Bill , 2026, was introduced in the House by Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry at a time when the daily fuel pricing mechanism has drawn widespread criticism. The bill seeks to insert a new Section 8A in the Ogra Ordinance, 2002. Under the proposed mechanism, a licensee for natural gas will submit its total revenue requirement on a quarterly basis — only to the extent of wellhead gas prices and the cost of imported gas, including Re-Gasified Liquefied Natural Gas (RLNG) — for review by the authority. Ogra will then advise the federal government, which must, within 30 days, advise minimum charges and sale prices for each category of retail consumer for gazette notification. The bill also empowers the federal government to advise Ogra to carry forward the entire or part of a quarterly adjustment to its forthcoming half-yearly determination under Section 8. In a clause likely to trigger debate, the bill amends Section 9 to state: “Provided that public hearing shall not be held by the Authority for revision of prescribed prices under Section 8A.” The statement of objects and reasons states that the primary objective is to align tariffs with market realities by adjusting for Rupee-Dollar parity in a timely manner, signal accurate pricing, curb accumulation of circular debt in the gas sector and ensure financial and operational stability of the gas supply chain. The bill landed in the Senate at a time when consumers are complaining of unpredictable fuel price shocks. If passed, it shall come into force at once. ‘Will Karachi’s sea be shifted next?’ During the Senate session on Friday, PPP Senator Waqar Mehdi raised the proposed shifting of Pakistan Petroleum Limited’s (PPL) head office from Karachi to Islamabad, warning that a pattern was emerging of moving federal headquarters, ministries and corporations away from Karachi. “The head office has been in Karachi since around 1951. Now attempts are being made to shift it to Islamabad through the board of directors, whose members are not elected representatives of the people,” Mehdi said. He pointed out that the current office’s rent was around Rs4 million per month, but shifting would cost billions. Around 500 officers and employees from Sindh work in PPL and would face severe economic and family disruption if the head office was moved, he said. “From the federal government’s conduct, it seems tomorrow they will talk of shifting Karachi’s sea to Islamabad as well,” Mehdi remarked. He said PPL’s core activities, exploration, imports and related infrastructure were linked to Karachi and the institution had been working successfully from there. He demanded the decision be withdrawn. PPP Senator Zamir Ghumro said oil and gas came under the domain of the Council of Common Interests (CCI). “How can you shift it without the will of the CCI?” he asked. In response, Chaudhry said PPL was a company and its board had repeatedly said vacating the office had become inevitable. “We take everything towards provincialism, regionalism. PPL’s assets are not only in Sindh but also in Balochistan. No employees are being affected. There is no provincialism in shifting this office from Karachi,” he said.

items.title: Des violences physiques aux violences silencieuses (Par Matel BOCOUM)
items.description: Malgré les dénonciations de toutes les formes de violence, quel qu’en soit l’auteur, les féminicides continuent de faire des victimes dans notre pays, dans un contexte marqué par la célébration de la campagne « Octobre rose ». Durant tout le mois, des stratégies de plaidoyer, de prévention et de lutte contre les cancers ont été déployées, avec pour objectifs d’alléger les souffrances des victimes et de leurs proches, de dissiper les craintes et de susciter des changements de comportement. Mais certains hommes ont assombri ce mois d’espoir. Leur jeu favori : donner un coup de pied dans la fourmilière, comme pour rappeler que, dans leur imaginaire, « la femme est leur propriété ». Les féminicides survenus en octobre ont ainsi donné un visage macabre à ce mois consacré à la sensibilisation et à la lutte contre les cancers féminins. Dans une chronique publiée en début de semaine sur sa plateforme digitale Mousso.sn, l’enseignante-chercheuse Fatoumata Bernadette Sonko déplore la précarité de la vie des femmes dans notre pays. Intitulée « Décidément, la vie des Sénégalaises n’est que vilénie », sa contribution dénonce cette vague de tueries, mais aussi l’inaction des autorités compétentes. « Mine de rien. Dans l’indifférence. La misogynie. Le féminicide continue à toquer à toutes les portes. En l’espace de 24 heures. Dans le même pays. Deux femmes tuées par deux hommes. Mame Diarra Sow, une coiffeuse de 24 ans, poignardée à mort à Thiès, et Aminata Sy, élève en classe de Terminale, âgée de 17 ans, retrouvée morte et ligotée dans un sac à Podor », déplore l’enseignante-chercheuse. Dans plusieurs localités, les femmes continuent de perdre la vie dans un contexte souvent marqué par des rapports sociaux inégalitaires et la prééminence masculine. Mais les violences ne se limitent pas aux agressions physiques. Les femmes subissent également des violences psychologiques et des souffrances silencieuses, parfois banalisées ou passées sous silence. La société ferme les yeux et peine à regarder certaines réalités en face. Le mois d’Octobre rose a également remis en lumière le sort de nombreuses femmes confrontées à la maladie. Certaines victimes du cancer du sein se retrouvent parfois abandonnées par leur partenaire. D’autres voient leur vie bouleversée par un cancer du col de l’utérus, lié, dans la grande majorité des cas, à une infection persistante par le papillomavirus humain (Hpv), qui peut se transmettre au sein du couple. D’autres encore, dans l’espoir de retenir leur partenaire ou de raviver son désir, recourent à des produits présentés comme aphrodisiaques, au risque de mettre leur santé en danger. Au Sénégal, le cancer du col de l’utérus figure parmi les principaux cancers touchant les femmes et constitue un problème majeur de santé publique. Selon l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (Oms), presque tous les cas de cancer du col de l’utérus sont liés à une infection persistante par des types de papillomavirus humains à haut risque. Les Hpv 16 et 18 sont notamment responsables d’une part importante de ces cancers. Cette maladie demeure une cause importante de morbidité et de mortalité chez les femmes. Les hommes, eux, ne développent ce type de cancer, mais sont néanmoins susceptibles de contracter le Hpv et le transmettre à leurs partenaires lors de rapports sexuels ou de contacts intimes. Les femmes peuvent ainsi contracter et transmettre ce virus. Dans leur plaidoyer, les médecins rappellent ainsi que la responsabilité des hommes ne saurait être éludée dans la lutte contre le cancer du col de l’utérus. Ils ne leur attribuent pas la responsabilité de la transmission du Hpv, puisque les deux partenaires peuvent être infectés, souvent sans présenter de symptômes. Il s’agit plutôt de souligner leur rôle dans la prévention et la protection de la santé de leurs partenaires, de les inciter à plus de bienveillance et de comportements sexuels responsables. Dans cette perspective, la vaccination ne devrait pas concerner uniquement les filles selon les spécialistes de la santé. Ils plaident pour la vaccination de la gent masculine en vue de prévenir les infections par le Hpv et de réduire sa circulation dans la population… matel.bocoum@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Education : l’UNESCO dote le Cameroun pour mieux piloter les apprentissages
items.description: © DR Le vendredi 30 octobre 2026, l’UNESCO a remis 25 ordinateurs portables et des équipements techniques à l’Équipe opérationnelle permanente et à l’Unité pilote des acquis scolaires. Objectif : renforcer le suivi, l’évaluation et la qualité de l’éducation au Cameroun. L’UNESCO renforce les capacités de pilotage et d’évaluation des apprentissages au Cameroun. Le vendredi 30 octobre 2026, l’organisation a officiellement remis des équipements informatiques à l’Équipe opérationnelle permanente (EOP) et à l’Unité pilote des acquis scolaires (UPAS). La dotation comprend 25 ordinateurs portables, des équipements d’impression et de projection, des logiciels spécialisés et des outils de travail collaboratif. La remise s’inscrit dans le cadre du Programme d’Appui à la Professionnalisation du Métier de l’Enseignant au Cameroun (PAPMEC). La cérémonie, marquée par la signature d’un accord de transfert de propriété avec le Ministère de l’Éducation de Base (MINEDUB), constitue une nouvelle avancée dans le renforcement des capacités nationales de coordination, de suivi et d’évaluation du système éducatif. Grâce à cette dotation, les équipes disposent désormais de moyens techniques supplémentaires pour améliorer le pilotage des activités du programme, faciliter le traitement et l’analyse des données sur les acquis scolaires et éclairer les décisions en faveur de la qualité des apprentissages. Réaffirmant l’engagement de l’UNESCO à accompagner les efforts nationaux, le Directeur et Représentant a.i. du Bureau régional de l’UNESCO pour l’Afrique centrale a souligné : « Pour l’UNESCO, cette démarche s’inscrit pleinement dans notre mandat de coopération avec les États membres, de renforcement des capacités nationales et de promotion d’une éducation inclusive et de qualité. » Financé par le Partenariat mondial pour l’éducation (GPE) et mis en œuvre conjointement par l’UNESCO et l’UNICEF, le PAPMEC accompagne les efforts du Gouvernement camerounais en faveur de la professionnalisation du métier d’enseignant et de l’amélioration de la qualité de l’éducation. Cet article Education : l'UNESCO dote le Cameroun pour mieux piloter les apprentissages est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Le LaNSA sensibilise les acteurs agroalimentaires des Savanes à la sécurité sanitaire des aliments
items.description: Dapaong, 30 oct. (ATOP) – Les producteurs, transformateurs et commerçants des produits agroalimentaires de la région des Savanes ont été sensibilisés aux exigences de la sécurité sanitaire des aliments et les missions de l’institution, le jeudi 29 octobre à Dapaong. Initiée par le Laboratoire national de la sécurité sanitaire et phytosanitaire des aliments (LaNSA), cette rencontre vise à renforcer la prévention des risques alimentaires, à protéger la santé des consommateurs et à contribuer à l’amélioration de la qualité des produits locaux. Au cours des échanges, le directeur général du LaNSA, Prof. Komla Sanda a expliqué que le laboratoire, créé en septembre 2025 par décret présidentiel, est chargé du contrôle de la qualité et de la sécurité sanitaire des aliments destinés à la consommation humaine et à l’alimentation animale. Il a attiré l’attention des participants sur les risques microbiologiques, susceptibles de provoquer des intoxications et des infections alimentaires aiguës, ainsi que les risques chimiques liés notamment aux métaux lourds, aux mycotoxines et aux résidus de pesticides. Prof. Sanda a indiqué que l’exposition prolongée à ces substances peut entraîner des maladies chroniques. «Au-delà du contrôle, le LaNSA accompagne les opérateurs économiques à travers des formations sur les bonnes pratiques d’hygiène et de fabrication, des conseils sur le choix des équipements et l’amélioration des procédés de transformation», a ajouté le directeur. Le secrétaire général du gouvernorat, Kegbero Latifou, a souligné les enjeux de la qualité des denrées alimentaires pour la santé des populations. Il a relevé les liens entre les habitudes alimentaires et certaines maladies, notamment les cancers et l’hypertension artérielle, invitant les acteurs à veiller à la salubrité des produits mis sur le marché. Il les a exhortés à se rapprocher du LaNSA pour s’informer sur les normes et les contrôles requis. Il a également rassuré les participants que des réflexions seront menées sur les coûts des prestations afin de faciliter l’accès aux services du laboratoire. Le professeur Komla Sanda a réaffirmé la disponibilité de son institution à poursuivre les échanges avec les opérateurs économiques afin d’adapter son accompagnement à leurs besoins et de transmettre aux autorités de tutelle leurs préoccupations relatives à la tarification des prestations. ATOP/JK/SED

items.title: Britain bars entry to Swedish academic ahead of appearance with Palestine Action founder
items.description: By Yoruk Bahceli LONDON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Swedish climate academic Andreas Malm said on Friday he had been denied entry to Britain, where he was due to speak alongside the co-founder of Palestine Action, a group banned as a terrorist organisation. Malm, an academic at Sweden's Lund University, has been a vocal critic of Israel and expressed strong support for the Palestinian movement. Britain's Home Office (interior ministry) said it did not comment on individual cases.

items.title: Citius, Altius, Fortius… (Par Oumar NDIAYE)
items.description: Accueil par le Sénégal des Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse, une première pour le continent africain, annonce du retour de la Formule 1 en Afrique avec le Rwanda, après une absence d’une trentaine d’années… Deux évènements qui, ces deux semaines, démontrent l’appropriation du levier sportif et son utilisation par les pays africains dans la conception de leur politique étrangère. Guidée par la défense des intérêts nationaux, qu’ils soient stratégiques et vitaux, la définition d’une politique étrangère par les États met en avant l’économie, la sécurité, entres autres. Aujourd’hui, elle insère des aspects comme le sport, la culture, la religion dans la projection de puissance et la recherche d’influence sur la scène internationale. La mise en avant du sport comme élément central et non périphérique dans la définition d’une politique étrangère sur le plan international n’est pas une donnée nouvelle, même si l’Afrique est en train de rattraper son retard dans ce domaine. Le Sénégal, en plus d’être le premier pays africain hôte d’une olympiade, celle de la Jeunesse, va aussi accueillir en 2031 les 11e Jeux de la Francophonie. Notre pays est aussi candidat pour l’organisation de la Coupe d’Afrique des Nations en 2032. Avec un tissu infrastructurel sportif devenu dense cette dernière décennie et surtout des performances des équipes nationales, notamment de football, vainqueur de deux Can, le Sénégal présente beaucoup d’atouts pour faire, à l’image du Maroc ou du Rwanda, du sport comme levier pour son nation branding. C’est connu et ressassé dans nos précédents écrits, l’organisation de compétitions sportives est aujourd’hui très prisée pour faire ce qui est appelé le « Nation branding ». Ce nouvel anglicisme très en vogue dans les études de marketing définit ainsi l’identité de marque d’une nation pour se vendre et se positionner à l’international. L’accueil de compétitions sportives internationales est ainsi perçu comme une consécration pour plusieurs pays qui veulent faire savoir qu’il faut désormais compter sur eux dans la marche de leur continent et du monde. Beaucoup de pays ont fait ce choix, de mettre en avant le sport, soit pour renforcer leur poids diplomatique ou encore pour polir leur image. En Afrique, le Rwanda est ainsi cité comme un adepte un sportwashing pour davantage relooké et lustré son image face aux accusations qui sont légion sur ce pays par rapport à la situation interne et sur sa participation aux conflits qui minent la région des Grands Lacs. Le branding « Visit Rwanda » est visible sur les maillots de plusieurs équipes européennes, de la Ligue 1 française à la Premier League anglais en passant par la Bundesliga et la Liga espagnol. Le Maroc est aussi des précurseurs de l’utilisation du sport comme moyen de renforcer son influence avec l’organisation réussie de la dernière Coupe d’Afrique des Nations, malgré la parenthèse malheureuse de la finale. Le Royaume s’apprête aussi à accueillir, avec l’Espagne et le Portugal, la prochaine Coupe du monde de football en 2030. « La puissance sportive peut accompagner la puissance stratégique ou lui servir de substitut, mais elle en est devenue un paramètre. Être une grande puissance implique de plus en plus d’avoir une vitrine sportive, faute de quoi la panoplie n’est pas complète », explique Pascal Boniface, dans son ouvrage « Géopolitique du Sport », paru en 2014 aux Éditions Arman Colin. C’est dire toute l’importance et la pertinence pour le Sénégal d’accueillir cette quatrième édition des Jeux olympiques de la Jeunesse. Que cet évènement soit chaleureux, merveilleux, et joyeux et réponde à l’esprit de l’olympisme tel que théorisé par Baron Pierre de Coubertin. Plus vite, plus haut, plus fort. Citius, Altius, Fortius… oumar.ndiaye@lesoleil.sn

items.title: La décrue des nationalistes (Par Ibrahima Khaliloullah NDIAYE)
items.description: Au pays de la Samba, la remontada se désigne par le mot « Virada ». C’est exactement la prouesse électorale que le président Lula a réussie. En se faisant réélire à près de 52 % des votes pour un quatrième mandat après un premier tour catastrophique, derrière son adversaire conservateur Flavio Bolsonaro. Belle performance pour Lula, 81 ans, sur qui, il y a 15 jours, peu de pronostiqueurs misaient. Le peuple des réseaux sociaux, — avec trois millions d’électeurs de plus qu’au second tour qui n’ont pas entendu se la faire raconter —, s’est déplacé en masse pour aller voter et enterrer les rêves de retour en force du clan Bolsonaro par la grande porte. C’est à croire que les réseaux sociaux ne jouent pas partout le même rôle. En France, Emmanuel Macron, tout naturellement agacé par les manifestations violentes en série, flétrissait, il y a quelques jours, ces mêmes réseaux sociaux en les accusant d’« abîmer la démocratie ». Au Brésil, le peuple des réseaux sociaux s’est levé comme un seul homme, au second tour, pour barrer la route au nationaliste Bolsonaro fils, digne héritier d’un père, Jair Bolsonaro, qui a failli enterrer la démocratie au Brésil en 2022, en voulant par la force des armes confisquer le pouvoir. Après Viktor Orban en Hongrie, il y a quelques mois, et le Premier ministre populiste serbe Aleksandar Vucic (battu cette semaine par le Mouvement des étudiants), c’est un bastion fort du nationalisme pro-Trump qui s’effondre avec la défaite de Bolsonaro. Pas surprenant que le président américain n’ait pas aimé du tout le résultat de l’élection présidentielle brésilienne qu’il a qualifiée de « lamentable » et « truquée ». « Franchement, ça ressemblait à une autre élection truquée… C’était tellement corrompu », a-t-il dit à des journalistes à Washington. La rivière nationaliste est en décrue par les temps qui courent. Avec le risque de baisser davantage aux États-Unis où les élections de mi-mandat risquent de ne pas être de tout repos pour Donald Trump qui pourrait perdre le contrôle du Congrès américain, fortement menacé par les Démocrates qui rêvent tout naturellement de prendre leur revanche dès cette année. Pendant que Flavio, le fugitif, débarque en réfugié politique aux États-Unis, son ami Donald prévient qu’il ne reconnaîtra les résultats des élections américaines de mi-mandat du 3 novembre seulement si… le « scrutin est honnête ». Reste à savoir ce qu’il faut mettre dans ce qualificatif. La décrue nationaliste commence à interroger. D’autant plus qu’en Israël, Netanyahou ne vit pas que des moments totalement tranquilles actuellement. Le vote de dimanche ne l’a pas fait perdre totalement mais… pas gagner aussi totalement. S’il venait à être battu, avec un Trump privé de la majorité parlementaire dans son pays, les choses pourraient être assez compliquées pour le camp de l’Internationale « nationaliste ». Bonne ou mauvaise nouvelle ? Bien évidemment, c’est selon. Mais des perspectives de relance du multilatéralisme éprouvé par les temps qui courent et d’apaisement des conflits au Moyen-Orient et pourquoi pas aussi en Europe, qui pour s’en plaindre ? Enfin… un célèbre penseur ne disait-il pas que « le bon sens est la chose du monde la mieux partagée » ? ibrahimakhalil.ndiaye@lesoleil.sn

items.title: 3e conférence régionale des OSC: «Nous refusons que la conservation se fasse au détriment des droits»
items.description: Deux jours ont servi aux organisations de la société civile ainsi qu’aux représentants des institutions étatiques du Bassin du Congo réunies à Libreville, pour poser les bases d’une position commune claire. À l'issue de la 3e Conférence régionale des organisations de la société civile du Bassin du Congo sous le thème « Un bassin du Congo résilient : forêts, populations, finances et nature », ils ont adopté une déclaration commune. Laquelle, défend entre autres, les droits des communautés. Scène de la remise de la déclaration de Libreville au ministre Ntossui. © GabonReview La 3e conférence des organisations de la société civile (OSC) du Bassin du Congo s'est achevée le 29 octobre à Libreville. Gouvernance forestière et gestion des ressources ; droits, savoirs, leadership et financement des peuples des forêts ; gouvernance de la biodiversité et résilience des écosystèmes ; financement climat et biodiversité : accès direct, équité et transparence. Les discussions ont porté sur plusieurs d’autant plus qu’environ 100 millions de personnes dépendent des forêts du Bassin du Congo. La rencontre s’inscrivait dans la continuité des conférences de Yaoundé 2024 et de Kinshasa en 2025, dont les analyses avaient porté sur la protection des forêts, la justice climatique, des droits des peuples des forêts et d’un accès équitable aux financements. Les échanges de Libreville ont permis de faire ressortir des solutions pour parvenir à l’équité souhaiter. Leur consolidation exige une volonté politique réelle, des moyens adaptés et la reconnaissance des communautés comme partie prenante à part entière de la gouvernance du bassin du Congo. « Nous refusons que la conservation se fasse au détriment des droits, que le développement des pays du bassin du Congo sacrifie les territoires villageois et que les financements destinés à protéger les forêts échappent à celles et ceux qui les préservent », soutient la déclaration de Libreville lue par le représentant des communautés locales Gabon, Dourani Toko Etienne. Au-delà des engagements déclaratifs Instantanés de la journée du 29 octobre. © GabonReview Les OSC ont donc appelé les gouvernements des pays du Bassin du Congo, les institutions régionales, les partenaires financiers et les entreprises à passer des engagements déclaratifs à des décisions vérifiables, assortis de responsabilité de moyens et d'échanges. Ce qui passe le renforcement de la gouvernance forestière en mettant fin à l'impunité ; la garantie de la transparence dans l'attribution des concessions forestières, minières, pétrolières et agro-industrielles ainsi que dans les décisions de déclassement ; la reconnaissance des droits, des savoirs et la diversité des peuples et des forêts. Mais aussi, la reconnaissance et la sécurisation des droits fonciers et forestiers coutumiers, en adaptant les cadres juridiques et les procédures afin que les territoires ancestraux soient identifiés, documentés et protégés contre les attributions incompatibles ou bien garantir une participation effective aux décisions en associant directement les peuples autochtones et les communautés locales à la conception, la négociation, la mise en œuvre et au suivi des projets qui concernent leur territoire et bien d’autres points. « Nous reconnaissons les avancées législatives et institutionnelles enregistrées dans plusieurs pays du bassin du Congo. Toutefois, l'existence des lois ne suffit pas lorsque leur application demeure insuffisante», ont souligné les OSC dans leur déclaration. Tenir compte des différents contextes Elles encouragent les États à examiner, selon les différents contextes nationaux, des mesures conservatoires, notamment des moratoires conditionnels sur l'attribution des nouveaux titres d'exploitation industrielle des ressources naturelles. À l'approche de la COP 31, les OSC invitent les gouvernements et les partenaires financiers à porter ces priorités dans les différents espaces de décision. « Nous réaffirmons que l'avenir du Bassin du Congo ne peut se construire sans celles et ceux qui vivent dans ces forêts », ont insisté les OSC dans leur déclaration. Pour la directrice exécutive de Greenpeace Africa, Dr Oulie Keita plusieurs priorités doivent guider le plaidoyer autour des différents points. Notamment, protéger les écosystèmes sensibles, garantir les droits des peuples autochtones et des communautés locales, renforcer la documentation des impacts environnementaux et sociaux, promouvoir les alternatives économiques durables, faciliter l'accès au financement climatique et environnemental pour les communautés et les organisations locales, renforcer la coopération régionale à travers un réseau permanent d'échanges. Le ministre des Eaux et Forêts, Maurice Ntossui Allogo mettant fin aux travaux, a reconnu que le financement climatique reste indispensable. Pour lui, la réussite de cette troisième édition de la conférence des OSC du bassin du Congo se mesurera à la capacité à traduire les orientations en changements concrets. « Le gouvernement de la Vème République prend acte de l'ensemble de ses recommandations avec la plus grande attention» , a-t-il déclaré. L’article 3e conférence régionale des OSC: «Nous refusons que la conservation se fasse au détriment des droits» est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: “They Killed Us”
items.description: Click to expand Image Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov of Russia during the award ceremony for the Nobel Peace prize on December 10, 2021, in Oslo, Norway. © 2021 Odd Andersen/AFP via Getty Images When I woke up this morning to the news that Novaya Gazeta is closing its doors, it felt like a personal blow. To me, Novaya’s office in a small grey building in central Moscow always felt like home. The newsroom moved to Moscow almost three decades ago. I got to know its every nook and cranny, as I went there, in my capacity of a Moscow-based Human Rights Watch researcher, for meetings, celebrations, commemorations, or simply to swap stories with a friendly journalist over coffee or wine. Click to expand Image Novaya Gazeta staff members with a portrait of Anna Politkovskaya" next to their office building in Moscow". © Novaya Gazeta archive I was there on the night of Anna Politkovskaya’s murder in October 2006 and stood outside seven years later as her memorial plaque was affixed to the wall. I celebrated with the newsroom when editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. For years, I worked alongside Novaya journalists in conflict zones. Together, we travelled to Chechnya, remote mountain villages in Dagestan, South Ossetia (Georgia), and Ukraine. It was more than collaboration; it was a true partnership. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the authorities set out to stifle Novaya Gazeta. By the end of 2022, the newspaper had lost its print and online media registrations, and its website had been blocked. Some journalists left Russia, launching Novaya Gazeta Europe and other projects in exile. Others stayed against all odds, continuing to publish investigations, interviews, and commentary online, accessible outside Russia and through circumvention tools inside the country. Despite mounting pressure, they persevered. In April 2026, police searched the newsroom for 13 hours and arrested a journalist on criminal charges carrying up to six years in prison. In September, the authorities designated Novaya Gazeta a “foreign agent” and listed over 100 staff and contributors as “affiliated individuals.” On October 29, the newspaper was told to vacate its offices. Its donation-processing system was also disabled, cutting off reader contributions. Today, Novaya Gazeta announced it would cease operations on November 9. In a statement titled “They Killed Us,” the editors wrote: “This is not just our own story. It is the story of a country and a society that are being destroyed in exactly the same way.” Novaya Gazeta’s story is also one of extraordinary courage and journalistic integrity. The authorities may silence a newspaper, but they cannot extinguish the voices of those who refuse to be silenced.

items.title: 2027: INEC receives over 4,800 claims, 600 objections on voter register
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has received over 4,800 claims and about 600 objections on the preliminary voter register, with a promise that the discrepancies will be corrected before the final register is certified on December 15, 2026. INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan SAN, disclosed this on Friday when the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Pre-Election Fact-Finding Mission paid a courtesy visit to the commission’s headquarters in Abuja. The mission is led by Victor Bockarie Foh, a former Vice-President of Sierra Leone. Amupitan said the claims, received at the registration areas where the register was displayed as of Thursday, were mainly corrections and other minor matters. On objections, he said the commission had received “about 600 complaints on the register” through electoral officers and Resident Electoral Commissioners from the various wards. He added that “the display of the register online is also confirming some of the complaints we had earlier received.” According to hum, the register now stands at over 103 million registered citizens, adding that it is a huge figure, and that the discrepancies noticed would be corrected so that “the register will be properly cleaned up” ahead of the final list. The commission completed three phases of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise and recently ended the physical display of the preliminary register at registration areas nationwide. It has also published the register on its online portal, display.inecnigeria.org, “for public scrutiny, claims, and objections.” He again restated that the Presidential and National Assembly elections will hold on Saturday, January 16, 2027, while the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections are scheduled for Saturday, February 6, 2027. He said the commission will deploy personnel and technology across 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, covering 774 Local Government Areas, 8,809 Registration Areas (Wards) and 176,846 polling units. Amupitan said the commission had executed nine of the 14 major milestones in its Revised Timetable and Schedule of Activities for the election. He said INEC had also moved “away from administrative assumptions” by personally conducting zonal readiness assessment tours. It has covered the South-West in Lagos, the North-West in Kaduna, the South-East in Enugu and the North-East in Gombe, and the team is heading to Port Harcourt for the South-South. The North-Central, the last zone, will be visited next week. He said the tours had shown that some areas needed higher deployments than planned because of terrain and security challenges. Amupitan disclosed that the commission is planning a mock accreditation across the country, which he said should hold “some time in November.” He said it would test accreditation and the transmission of results simultaneously in all the states, to be sure the commission can “cure the problem of glitch that took place in 2023.” On technology, he said the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) will be deployed for dual biometric accreditation, by fingerprint and face. The commission has also introduced a new electronic verification platform, eEC8A, for results transmitted to the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV). He said a safeguard has been introduced so that results are authenticated at the polling unit before they go to the portal. He explained that discrepancies had emerged in the past as results moved from the polling unit to higher levels of collation. On staff welfare, Amupitan said the commission had secured approval for the Consolidated Election Management Body Salary Structure, which takes its workforce out of the regular civil service scale. It also secured a 150 per cent increase in state operational overheads. In return, he said, the commission maintains “zero tolerance for administrative negligence, extortion, or partisan compromise.” That policy is backed by Oaths of Neutrality under Section 26 of the Electoral Act 2026. On security, he said the commission is working with the Nigeria Police Force, the Department of State Services, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps and the Armed Forces through the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES). The framework uses early risk-mapping tools to secure polling units, protect ad-hoc staff, particularly members of the National Youth Service Corps, and guarantee access for all voters, including persons with disabilities. He said the commission is also finalising plans for internally displaced persons, “to ensure inclusivity.” Amupitan, who said he has been in office for one year, having been sworn in on October 23 last year, said the commission had conducted four main off-cycle elections and 16 by-elections in that period. He said these gave INEC the chance to test its plans and equipment. “The mistakes of the past cannot be allowed to repeat themselves,” he said. He told the ECOWAS delegation the commission welcomes the deployment of long-term and short-term ECOWAS election observation missions. “We welcome your scrutiny. INEC has no candidate and no political party. Our sole allegiance is to the rule of law, the sovereign will of the Nigerian electorate, and the democratic progress of our nation”, he said. items.title: Ligue 1 Pro Orange : Le championnat reprend ses droits
items.description: © Internet Initialement prévu le 10 octobre 2026, le coup d’envoi de la Ligue 1 Pro Orange 2026-2027 sera donné ce samedi 31 octobre. Après un premier report demandé par les clubs, les quatorze formations de l’élite s’apprêtent à retrouver la compétition, avec plusieurs affiches intéressantes dès la première journée. Quatorze ans après la dernière participation d’un club de Kayes au championnat national, la ville retrouve l’élite du football malien. Cette fois, elle sera représentée par l’AS Kayes, qui découvre la Ligue 1 pour la première fois de son histoire. Le promu accueillera l’US Bougouba le 31 octobre en match d’ouverture de la saison. La reprise intervient trois semaines après la date initialement retenue. Le report, officialisé le 6 octobre par la Fédération malienne de football (FEMAFOOT), avait été sollicité par les clubs, dont plusieurs joueurs étaient mobilisés pour le tournoi UFOA-A U20 organisé à Bamako. Des affiches relevées d’entrée Sur le plan sportif, le Djoliba AC abordera l’exercice dans la peau du Champion sortant. Sacrés avec 59 points la saison dernière, les Rouges tenteront de conserver leur couronne face à une concurrence emmenée par le Stade malien, deuxième avec 50 points, et l’AS Réal, troisième avec 49 unités. Le FC Diarra, quatrième du précédent championnat, voudra également confirmer sa progression. Le calendrier de la première journée réserve d’ailleurs deux oppositions de premier plan. L’AS Réal accueillera le Stade malien le 1 er novembre dans un duel entre prétendants au titre. Le lendemain, le FC Diarra sera opposé au Djoliba AC pour des retrouvailles après leur confrontation en Supercoupe, remportée par les Rouges début octobre. Les autres rencontres mettront aux prises Binga FC et l’USFAS, ainsi que l’AS Bakaridjan et Afrique Football Élite, le 1 er novembre. L’ASKO affrontera Derby Académie le 2, tandis que les Onze Créateurs de Niaréla recevront l’autre promu, le Centre sportif de Bamako. Pour les deux promus, l’enjeu sera surtout de réussir leurs premiers pas dans l’élite. L’AS Kayes et le Centre sportif de Bamako devront rapidement trouver leurs repères face à des adversaires plus expérimentés, avec pour première ambition d’assurer leur maintien. Outre les résultats, cette reprise s’accompagne de nouvelles attentes sur le plan organisationnel. La FEMAFOOT a porté de 25 à 40 millions de francs CFA la subvention annuelle accordée à chaque club. Ce soutien supplémentaire intervient alors que la professionnalisation continue de soulever des questions de financement, d’infrastructures et de gestion. Mohamed Kenouvi

items.title: 37e Tour du Faso 2026: Tom Wijfje frappe fort d’entrée, Souleymane Koné décroche la deuxième place
items.description: Le Néerlandais Tom Wijfje a remporté, ce vendredi 30 octobre 2026, la première étape de la 37e édition du Tour international du Faso, courue sur 152,15 kilomètres entre Ouagadougou et Kaya. Le Burkinabè Souleymane Koné s’est illustré en terminant deuxième, tandis que son compatriote Paul Daumont a pris la cinquième place. Le ton est donné sur les routes du Tour du Faso 2026. Pour cette première explication entre les coureurs, le Néerlandais Tom Wijfje a réussi une entrée en matière remarquable en s’adjugeant la victoire de l’étape inaugurale, disputée entre la capitale burkinabè et Kaya, sur une distance de 152,15 kilomètres. Derrière le coureur hollandais, le Burkinabè Souleymane Koné a réalisé une belle performance en s’emparant de la deuxième place. Une prestation qui permet au cyclisme national de se signaler dès les premiers coups de pédale de cette compétition internationale. Paul Daumont, lui termine la course en se classant à la cinquième position. Avec deux représentants parmi les cinq premiers de cette étape inaugurale, les Étalons cyclistes affichent de bonnes dispositions face à leurs adversaires étrangers. De quoi nourrir des espoirs pour la suite de cette 37e édition. La compétition ne fait toutefois que commencer. Les coureurs burkinabè sont désormais attendus sur les prochaines étapes pour confirmer cette belle entame et poursuivre la bataille pour les premières places du classement général. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article 37e Tour du Faso 2026: Tom Wijfje frappe fort d’entrée, Souleymane Koné décroche la deuxième place est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .
